newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador Congress to meet, Bucaram under threat.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador Congress to meet, Bucaram under threat.

text.p: The speaker of Ecuador's Congress called legislators to a special session on Thursday where opponents may seek to fire President Abdala Bucaram amid severe social unrest.
Protesters on the second day of a 48-hour general strike, angered by tough austerity measures and scorning the president's eccentric behaviour, were calling for Congress to depose Bucaram.
Speaker Fabian Alarcon refused to say whether Congress would seek to depose the president at the special session scheduled to start at 6 p.m. (2300 GMT) on Thursday.
"We still cannot speak of such and such a solution or resolution of Congress. That will be worked out by all the legislators," Alarcon said, "This evening we will have a session of great importance."
But a top Bucaram supporter said the government was lobbying Congress hard to avoid a vote to fire the president.
"We are putting together a majority. We are sure we are going to make it," said Monetary Board president Alvaro Noboa.
Alarcon told reporters on Wednesday that he had received threats that Congress would be dissolved if deputies met to discuss deposing Bucaram.

The speaker declined to say who had made the threats, but a senior congressional official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters that Bucaram had threatened to dissolve Congress and have Alarcon arrested.

Alarcon called for popular support: "I invite the Ecuadoran people to come to Congress peacefully, but actively and energetically to ensure that the democratic will of the country is respected," he said.

The government declared a "state of mobilisation" on the first day of the strike, and sent a squad of soldiers to surround Congress. Their commanding officer said they had come to protect legislators from mobs.
Of Congress's 82 members, 19 are members of Bucaram's Roldosista Party, while another 12 are government allies.

Government sources said that 55 congressmen would have to vote for Bucaram to be fired to depose him, but opposition members said they would only need 42 votes. If Congress did vote to remove Bucaram, the post of president would be declared vacant.
After sometimes violent clashes with police on Wednesday, workers and students on Thursday began the second day of the general strike with marches throughout the mountainous nation.
Dressed for morning cold in the Andean provinces, or in shirtsleeves in the tropical lowlands, the strikers manned roadblocks and burned tires in provincial cities.

Road traffic was returning to normal in the capital Quito, but public transport was scarce and expected to get more so as the day wore on. "There are marches planned for the afternoon, and we aren't going to risk our vehicles," said a bus driver.
Truck drivers went on strike on Monday, causing shortages of food and fuel in some parts of the country.

Ecuador, a country of 11.7 million people, has suffered social unrest since Bucaram's six-month-old government launched an austerity package including hikes in electricity, telephone and public transportation rates in January.

Bucaram's tendency to name friends and family members to important posts and his flamboyant personality also came under fire from the opposition. Nicknamed "El Loco" -- "madman" in Spanish -- he released a rock-and-roll record soon after taking office and his antics included shaving off his moustache on live television.

Organisation of American States (OAS) Secretary General Cesar Gaviria flew to Ecuador after an urgent request for mediation from Bucaram. But after meeting the president he told journalists late on Wednesday he would not mediate.
